 Trump administration Trump’s pick for agency providing election security says Jan. 6 was not an attack
 Michael LoSapio, the president’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, would not say who won the 2020 presidential election. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Michael LoSapio, who serves as the chief information security officer at Palantir, was also asked whether there was an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 19, 2026, 5:22 PM EST By Kyla Guilfoil The nominee selected by President Donald Trump to lead the agency tasked with protecting elections in the U.S. refused Thursday to answer who won the 2020 presidential election or call the riot on Jan. 6, 2021, “an attack.” 
 Michael LoSapio, who is nominated to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, was pressed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on the issues during a confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. 
 Asked specifically who won the presidential race in 2020, LoSapio said, “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago.” 
 “My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States,” he added, referencing Trump. 
 Blumenthal accused LoSapio of “ducking the question in a way that betrays your lack of independence and objectivity.” 
 CISA has not had a director confirmed by the Senate since Trump returned to office in January 2025, when Jen Easterly vacated the role. 
 The agency, which was established during the first Trump administration, was meant to protect the country’s critical infrastructure, including its elections, from hackers or cybercriminals.

 Slide 1 of 1 LoSapio, who serves as the chief information security officer at data and software company Palantir, was also asked whether there was an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6.
 Blumenthal pressed him on the issue, saying, “You don’t know?” 
 “No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said. “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.” 
 Blumenthal asked LoSapio about the nature of the riot once again, to which he maintained that “it was not an attack.”

 Slide 1 of 1 Trump’s own account of Jan. 6 has changed over the years , as he initially sought to distance himself from the riot, calling what happened “acts of violence and destruction” on Jan. 7, 2021.
 Though, as he hit the campaign trail in 2024, Trump shifted gears to call it a “day of love,” and later, when he returned to office, he pardoned roughly 1,500 people and commuted the sentences of another 14 in connection with the attack. Trump’s Justice Department also tried to launch a controversial “anti-weaponization” fund earlier this year to compensate Trump allies. 
 LoSapio is one of 13 nominees who appeared before the committee Thursday seeking to take over federal oversight, inspector general, Postal Service and District of Columbia Superior Court positions.
 To be confirmed as CISA director, LoSapio requires the committee to vote to advance his nomination to the full Senate, whose vote by a simple majority will determine whether he is confirmed. The clock is ticking for Trump nominees, as Democrats will take over control of Congress in January. 
 The result of the 2020 presidential election has shaped CISA’s leadership. Trump fired its first director , Chris Krebs, just weeks after the election over his assertion that it was a secure race. 
 LoSapio isn’t the first Trump nominee to skirt around questions regarding 2020’s presidential race. 
 On Wednesday, Cody Hiland, Trump’s pick for a federal appeals court seat, told Blumenthal, “I’m not going to answer that,” when asked who won the election.
 Asked why he would not answer, Hiland said, “Because it’s going down a political track on an issue that happened six years ago, and I don’t want to come close to an ethical violation.” 
 “We know the White House told you, ‘Don’t answer that question,’” Blumenthal responded.
